meta.program: Own Your 1:1 · Take-Off Tuesday · Anchor's Edge · Vanderbilt
meta.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; nobody is assumed to manage anyone. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. Oracle access helps, and the session works fine watching the walkthrough.
meta.roomSetup: Virtual, instructor led: camera on, deck link in chat, breakouts of 2 available. Learners follow on their own screens via the welcome-slide link or QR. Nothing typed into the deck is saved or sent.
meta.postSession: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did your item make it into a 1:1 template? Did you send or give one piece of feedback through Oracle? What changed because it was on the record?' Count of template entries and feedback events is the month's usage signal.

full.description: The full 45-minute virtual session: every interaction runs live, breakouts run in pairs, and the capstone gets read-alouds. The per-section minutes on each slide sum to 45 including transitions.

core.description: The 30-minute slot: agenda and core-idea slides pass in stride, breakouts become solo passes with chat share-outs, debriefs shrink to one voice. Never cut the section interactions or the capstone.

meta.framework: ATD facilitator-guide structure: per module SAY / DO / ASK (with anticipated responses) / DEBRIEF / TRANSITION, plus preparation checklists, materials, contingencies, and a tough-questions bank.
materials: Meeting platform with screen share and breakout rooms; deck link ready to paste in chat
Facilitator machine with the facilitator edition open; notifications off
Learners on their own devices with the learner link
Chat open for share-outs; the capstone copy button pastes there cleanly

weekBefore: Run the learner edition start to finish and do every interaction honestly; you will demo at least one live.
Read this month's theme page on the Anchor's Edge dashboard so the goal tie-in is fluent.
Send the invite with the learner link and one line on what to bring.
dayBefore: Test screen share with the facilitator edition; confirm the notes rail is readable.
Open the learner link on a second device; the QR must land there.
Run the section interactions once so you can drive them without reading.
thirtyMinBefore: Welcome slide up as people join; link pasted in chat.
Close every other tab; silence the machine.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Learners lack Oracle access or cannot open it during the session
contingencies.then: Nothing requires live Oracle. Demo from your own screen, and have people draft their agenda item and feedback lines in the deck; entering them takes two minutes after the call.

contingencies.if: Someone starts naming a colleague while describing feedback they want to give
contingencies.then: Redirect warmly: roles, never names. The specifics belong in the tool, addressed to the person; the room only needs the shape of the example.

toughQuestions.q: What if my manager never opens the template?
toughQuestions.a: Your entry still works: it frames the meeting when you bring it up, and it timestamps that you raised it. Most managers start using the template the week their reports do. If it stays ignored, raise that kindly as its own agenda item.

toughQuestions.q: Is feedback I give in Oracle visible to the person and their manager?
toughQuestions.a: Treat everything in the tool as on the record; that is the point, because recorded recognition travels. Write anything you give as words you would happily say with the person in the room, since functionally you are.

toughQuestions.q: I don't manage anyone. Is this month really for me?
toughQuestions.a: Entirely. The manager standard tells you what to expect from your own manager, and the tools are two-sided by design; this month lands only if both chairs use them. If you are curious where the manager side goes, the New Manager Foundations course on LinkedIn Learning is open to everyone.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Tuesday, 45 minutes on making Oracle 1:1s work for you. Before the session, think of one item you keep meaning to raise with your manager. You will never be asked to share it. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did it make the record? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did your item make it into a 1:1 template? 2) Did you send or give one piece of feedback in Oracle? 3) What changed because it was on the record?

sections.title: Welcome / QR
sections.purpose: Get everyone into the deck on their own screen and set the tone: 45 minutes, live, hands on.
sections.say: Welcome to Take-Off Tuesday. Scan the code or click the link in chat so this session runs on your screen too. Forty-five minutes, one focus: The 1:1 templates and feedback tools inside Oracle, from your side of the table.
facilitate: Slide up as people join; link pasted in chat every few minutes.
State the norm once: type into your own screen, nothing you enter is saved or sent.
sections.watchFor: People lurking without the deck open. The interactions only land if the deck is on their screen.
sections.transition: Before the topic, thirty seconds on why Vanderbilt is asking for this hour.

sections.title: The mission
sections.purpose: Anchor the session in the Chancellor's charge so the next 40 minutes read as mission work, not admin.
sections.say: This year of learning hangs off one sentence from the Chancellor: Vanderbilt will define the great university of the 21st Century and be it. The great university of the 21st Century runs on conversations that go somewhere. When any staff member can steer a 1:1 and put feedback on the record, Exceptional Core Operations shows up one meeting at a time.
facilitate: Read the mission line slowly, once.
Point at the tie-in line and let it sit; no discussion needed here.
sections.transition: That is the why. Here is the number we are moving.

sections.title: The goal we are targeting
sections.purpose: Name the enterprise goal this month serves.
sections.say: Every month of Anchor's Edge lands on one of three enterprise goals. This month is Goal 2, Manager Effectiveness at Scale: Implement a Vanderbilt manager standard that measures demonstrated leader behavior. Goal 2 asks managers to demonstrate a standard, and much of it becomes visible inside Oracle's 1:1 and feedback tools. Today you learn your half of those tools.
facilitate: Read the goal once, plainly.
One line, not a lecture: this session is one of the moves that serves it.
sections.transition: Here is what you will be able to do in 45 minutes.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.purpose: Set the contract for the session in under a minute.
sections.say: By the end of this session: load your own agenda items into the oracle 1:1 template before the meeting; give and request feedback through the oracle tools with specifics that help; capture commitments in the shared record and make it argue for your growth. That is the whole contract.
facilitate: Read the three objectives briskly; do not elaborate yet.

sections.title: Agenda
sections.purpose: Show the path so the room can pace itself.
sections.say: Three stops: the template, the feedback tools, the record. Each one has something to play with, so keep the deck open.
facilitate: Point once at each stop; ten seconds each.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the read-through, gesture at the slide in passing.

sections.title: The template
sections.purpose: Get every learner to load their own items into the Oracle 1:1 template before the meeting.
sections.say: Quick show of honesty in chat: when your last 1:1 started, whose agenda was it? For most of us the honest answer is my manager's, or nobody's. Oracle now gives that meeting a shared template both people can edit, and the single highest-leverage habit in this session is typing your two items into it the day before: one blocker, one growth topic.
facilitate: Show the template fields on screen for thirty seconds; keep it to where your items go.
Walk the In the room context; let the whose-agenda question sit. No quiz in the live room.
Open the discussion prompt; take two or three voices before moving on.
Run the breakout on the saved-up item.

ask.q: What stops people from adding their own agenda items?
expect: Assume the manager owns the meeting
ask.respond: All common, all fixable. The template design is the permission: the field exists for you, and managers consistently say they want the items.

sections.debrief: Two items, typed the day before: one blocker, one growth ask. That habit alone changes what 1:1s do for you.
sections.watchFor: Learners whose managers do not yet use the template. Acknowledge it and stay practical: your typed items work even when you are the only one typing.
sections.transition: The template covers the meeting. Feedback has its own front door.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for saved-up items in chat instead.

sections.title: The feedback tools
sections.purpose: Teach when to request feedback, when to give it, and when a topic belongs on the 1:1 agenda instead.
sections.say: Oracle gives everyone two feedback moves. Request: you ask people who saw your work how it landed, and their answers join your record. Give: you put specific recognition or input into a colleague's record, where it travels further than chat ever will. The skill is matching the moment to the move, so let's practice on three.
facilitate: Run Pick the move live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round two, ask in chat who has ever received recorded feedback from a peer; notice the energy.
Run the breakout on the colleague whose work deserved a recorded give.

ask.q: Why does recorded feedback beat the same words in chat?
ask.respond: All three. The words might be identical; the address is different. Feedback in the record shows up when decisions about people get made.

sections.debrief: Request when you need eyes on your work. Give when a colleague earned it. Anything needing real discussion goes on the 1:1 agenda.
sections.watchFor: Worry that requesting feedback signals weakness. Reframe it: asking specific people about specific work reads as someone serious about getting better.
sections.transition: Templates and feedback both feed one thing: a record. The last section makes it work for you.
sections.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the chat question.

sections.title: The record
sections.purpose: Convert template and feedback habits into a growth trail: agendas in, commitments out.
sections.say: Play the long game for a second. A year from now, someone will ask what you have grown into, in a review or an internal interview. The strongest answer is a trail: agendas you set, commitments that closed, feedback you asked for and acted on. Trails get built one meeting at a time, so let's set up your next one properly.
facilitate: Run Set up your next 1:1; give the room two minutes for both choices.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: typed beats mental, shared beats private.

ask.q: What does a shared commitment have that a private note does not?
ask.respond: Right. A private note protects your memory; a shared commitment obligates two calendars. Growth lives in the second kind.

sections.debrief: The record is your career's paper trail. Feed it: items in before, commitments out after, feedback along the way.
sections.watchFor: Anyone treating the record as surveillance. The frame is ownership: this is your trail, built by you, arguing for you.
sections.transition: Quick recap, then you load your own next 1:1.
sections.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.purpose: Land the one sentence the session exists to install.
sections.say: If you keep one sentence from today, this is it. Read it once, out loud: A 1:1 you prepared for is a meeting you co-own.
facilitate: Pause two beats after reading; the word animation carries it.
sections.coreNote: Core: pass through in stride; the sentence reads itself.

sections.title: Recap quiz
sections.purpose: Score the learning while it is fresh; wrong answers are teaching moments, not failures.
sections.say: Three questions, on your own screen. Answer honestly; the explanations are where the learning sticks.
facilitate: Give the room 90 seconds to run it individually.
Ask for a show of results in chat: how many got 3 of 3?
Read out the explanation for whichever question drew the most misses.
sections.watchFor: Rushing past the why lines. The explanations carry the teaching.
sections.transition: Now point it at your real week.

sections.title: Capstone commitment
sections.purpose: Convert the session into one named, dated action per person.
sections.say: Now load the real thing. Your next 1:1 is on a calendar somewhere. Name the item you have been sitting on, pick your first move, pick your window, and build the card. Roles only, never names. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitate: Two quiet minutes; everyone builds their own card.
Invite two or three volunteers to read their card aloud or paste it in chat.
Remind: copy the card somewhere you will see it this week.
sections.watchFor: Vague entries. Nudge for a name-able situation and a real date.

sections.title: Closing
sections.purpose: End with the next step and where this thread continues.
sections.say: You leave with a loaded template habit and two feedback moves that put your work on the record. Thursday's Thrive Thursday is the skill underneath every one of these tools: clarity, the kind of expectation-setting that sticks, whichever chair you sit in. Same time, same rhythm. See you there.
facilitate: Point at the next-step card; one sentence.
Name the rest of the week's rhythm: the other sessions echo this month's theme.
